options.text: The joining of two light nuclei
The absorption of gamma radiation by a nucleus
The emission of an alpha particle from a nucleus
The splitting of a large nucleus into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons

questions.explanation: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus (such as uranium-235) into two smaller nuclei, releasing neutrons and a large amount of energy.

questions.stem: What is needed to start fission in a uranium-235 nucleus?

options.text: A gamma ray
An alpha particle
An electron
A neutron

questions.explanation: Fission in uranium-235 is initiated when the nucleus absorbs a neutron. This makes it unstable, and it splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and typically 2-3 more neutrons.

questions.stem: What is a chain reaction in nuclear fission?

options.text: A reaction that absorbs energy rather than releasing it
A reaction that only happens once
A reaction where the neutrons released by one fission event cause further fission events
A chemical reaction between uranium and oxygen

questions.explanation: A chain reaction occurs when the neutrons released by one fission event are absorbed by other nuclei, causing them to split and release more neutrons, which cause further fission events, and so on.

questions.stem: What is the role of control rods in a nuclear reactor?

options.text: To cool the reactor core
To absorb excess neutrons and keep the chain reaction at a steady rate
To shield workers from radiation
To provide the fuel for fission

questions.explanation: Control rods (made of boron or cadmium) absorb excess neutrons. By raising or lowering them, operators can control the rate of the chain reaction, keeping it steady for safe power generation.

questions.stem: Which fuel is commonly used in nuclear fission reactors?

options.text: Carbon
Helium
Uranium-235 or plutonium-239
Hydrogen

questions.explanation: Uranium-235 and plutonium-239 are the most commonly used fission fuels. Their large, unstable nuclei are capable of sustaining a chain reaction when bombarded with neutrons.

questions.stem: What is the function of the moderator in a nuclear reactor?

options.text: To provide shielding from radiation
To speed up the neutrons
To absorb all the neutrons
To slow down the neutrons so they are more likely to cause fission

questions.explanation: The moderator (typically water or graphite) slows down the fast neutrons released during fission. Slow (thermal) neutrons are much more likely to be absorbed by uranium-235 and cause further fission.

questions.stem: Where does the energy released in nuclear fission come from?

options.text: From the gravitational potential energy of the nucleus
From chemical bonds between atoms
From a small amount of mass being converted into energy (E = mc squared)
From the kinetic energy of the neutrons only

questions.explanation: The total mass of the products is slightly less than the total mass of the reactants. This small mass difference is converted into a large amount of energy according to Einstein's equation E = mc squared.
